findings.matters: Shows council willing to discontinue services rather than manage deficits. Finance directors watch peer service decisions during budget pressure; lenders track whether councils are pruning non-core activities.

findings.detail: £1m saving from CSG contract expiry. Services are being reprocured through a mix of discrete third-party contracts and in-house delivery. IT elements are being insourced rather than continuing the outsourced arrangement, signalling a directional shift from outsourcing.
findings.matters: Major contract transition happening immediately; peers observe how others manage large contract exits. findings.detail: Replaces existing Revenues function contract with cost reductions phased across the period: £1.7m in 2028/29, £480k in 2029/30, and £2.18m in 2031/32. Reflects contract renegotiation or respecification delivering efficiency gains in a core transactional service.
findings.matters: Largest single-line efficiency saving in the plan, affecting a transactional service common across all councils. Finance directors track peer performance on contract cost reduction. Lenders monitor whether councils are realizing contracted savings.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals

findings.detail: The only positive variance shown across the savings plan. While most contracts are scrutinised for efficiency, GLL is projected to over-deliver against income assumptions. This represents operational performance outperformance on a major council services contract.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost control includes occupancy audit pilot to identify non-occupied units and pursue evictions
findings.detail: £2.035m in TA savings span housing options redesign, mediation, occupancy checks, and move-ons from expensive placements. Council is explicitly deploying occupancy audits to identify non-occupancy and sub-letting in both private and in-house stock, with a view to pursuing eviction proceedings to free properties for households in housing need. Pilot data shows 76 percent of outcomes sustained for 14 months.
findings.matters: Shows how council is implementing direct occupancy recovery as a cost control measure. Finance directors across councils dealing with TA growth will watch this approach; lenders track whether councils are managing growing TA exposure through active intervention.
findings.figures: £2,035m total TA savings; 3,036 units in use end May 2026; 76 percent of occupancy-check outcomes sustained for 14 months; 69 percent of TA stock is emergency nightly-paid or block-booked
findings.quote: In these cases, Barnet Homes may be able to pursue eviction proceedings, to free up properties that can be re-let to households who have a pressing housing need.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Savings & Income Generation Proposals
findings.headline: £21.2m savings plan is frontloaded to 2027/28 with £7.863m needed in first year, while some savings depend on pilot programmes continuing
findings.detail: Proposals total £21.204m over five years, with £7.863m (37%) concentrated in 2027/28, then only £2.459m in 2028/29. Several initiatives are explicit one-year pilots or contingent on external funding. Early Help Prevention Officer funding depends on sub-regional support ceasing at end 2026/27, creating a structural dependency.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to know whether savings are baselined or contingent, and whether their concentration in year one creates delivery risk. The dependency on pilot continuation and external funding changes creates pressure-bid exposure.
findings.figures: £21,204m total; £7,863m in 2027/28; cost avoidance £4,495m (21 percent of total); cost recovery maximisation £4,556m

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: Council developing Financial Sustainability Plan with prevention and cost-driver focus, to be presented October 2026
findings.detail: The council has developed a Financial Sustainability Plan to be presented to Cabinet in October 2026, introducing a cost-driver-led approach. The plan focuses on prevention (identifying and tackling root causes of demand using predictive analytics) and working smarter (reducing avoidable demand and duplication), supported by five delivery blocks, three enabling blocks, and governance and benefits realisation arrangements.
findings.matters: This is the council's formal strategy to exit Exceptional Financial Support; its credibility and execution will determine whether the March 2029 sustainability target is achievable.
findings.figures: Plan presentation October 2026; sustainability target March 2029
findings.quote: We have developed a Plan for Financial Sustainability which will be published in October.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: All of council's most significant risks (scoring 25 and 20) are finance-related, covering financial sustainability, HRA viability, and capital programme
findings.detail: The council's most significant risks in Q4 2025/26 are entirely finance-related: Financial Sustainability (25), HRA viability capital and revenue (25 each, both new to register), Capital Programme (20), Equal Pay claim (20), and Gas prices (20). Of 189 total risks recorded, 67 were finance risks, with 15 scoring high-level severity (15+). This concentration shows leadership has identified financial resilience as the dominant organisational challenge.
findings.matters: The absence of operational or governance risks at the highest severity level, with finance dominating entirely, shows the primary organisational challenge is financial resilience not service delivery failure.
findings.figures: Q4: 189 total risks; 67 finance risks (35%); 15 high-level finance risks (22%)
findings.quote: The council's most significant risks (scoring 25 and 20) were all Finance risks (see table below), relating to financial sustainability and resilience.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: Escalating demand in Children's Social Care, Adults' Social Care, SEND, and homelessness/temporary accommodation identified as primary pressure
findings.detail: The S151 officer identified escalating demand in these high-cost services as a core financial pressure for 2026/27. The council simultaneously faces persistent inflation in care markets and utilities, and significant workforce pressures including recruitment and retention challenges in statutory services.
findings.matters: These are the council's highest-cost services; understanding where demand is escalating shows where financial stress concentrates and which cost drivers must be tackled.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: Escalating demand pressures, particularly within Children's Social Care, Adults' Social Care, SEND, and homelessness/temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: Council faces structural budget gaps from demand exceeding resources with limited scope for further efficiency savings without material service impact
findings.detail: The S151 officer identified structural budget gaps emerging from demand outstripping available resources. Importantly, the officer reported limited opportunities for further efficiencies without material service impacts, indicating the council has exhausted conventional cost-reduction options and must address root causes of demand.
findings.matters: Exhaustion of efficiency headroom means the council cannot rely on conventional budget-tightening to close gaps; structural solutions are required and options are narrowing.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: Structural budget gaps emerging from demand outstripping available resources; Limited opportunities for further efficiencies without material service impacts

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: S151 officer assessed unallocated reserves as too low for managing risks and uncertainties, with replenishment a future priority
findings.detail: In assessing reserve adequacy, the S151 officer explicitly stated that current levels of unallocated reserves are insufficient for managing normal risks and uncertainties. Rebuilding reserves has been identified as a critical strategic priority once the council achieves financial sustainability, but this is conditional on first closing the deficit.
findings.matters: The council's own finance officer has explicitly stated current reserves are inadequate for normal risk management, meaning the council has reduced buffer capacity for demand shocks or delivery failures.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: Current levels of unallocated reserves for managing risks and uncertainties were too low but replenishment of reserves in future years must be a priority for the council

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve at £15m conditional on earmarked reserves being rebuilt to £40m 'as soon as possible'
findings.detail: The S151 officer maintained the General Fund Reserve at £15m, considered prudent given specific risks, but with an important condition: this adequacy is dependent on earmarked reserves being replenished to at least £40m as soon as possible. The language ('as soon as possible') indicates minimum buffers dependent on successful rebuilding.
findings.matters: Conditional reserve adequacy and urgency language signal tight buffers and vulnerability to demand shocks.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve £15m; earmarked reserves target £40m
findings.quote: The level of General Fund Reserve is maintained at £15m which the Section 151 considered was a prudent level in recognising the specific risks, although this was reliant on earmarked reserves being replenished up to at least the Council approved level of £40m as soon as possible

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: Council dependent on Exceptional Financial Support from government with target to reach financial sustainability by March 2029
findings.detail: The S151 officer reported that the council's financial position entering 2026/27 remained extremely challenging, with escalating demand pressures, persistent inflation, and workforce challenges. With government Exceptional Financial Support, the council has short-term arrangements to fulfil statutory duties, but recognises that EFS is not a long-term solution and must take significant steps to reduce expenditure or generate additional income.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer councils need to understand the council's reliance on emergency government support and its exit strategy; this defines the fundamental constraint on financial resilience and timeline for resolution.
findings.figures: Target to become financially sustainable by March 2029
findings.quote: With EFS from Government, the council had, short term, arrangements to fulfil its statutory duties.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Fair Funding Reforms structure penalizes Barnet for strong tax base and historic low council tax, creating structural underfunding
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Fair Funding Reforms use a notional council tax to assess councils' local income-raising capacity. Barnet has a large tax base and has historically maintained one of the lowest council tax rates in London. The FFR framework assumes councils in this position should raise more locally and therefore allocates them less grant. This creates a dual disadvantage: lower central government support because the FFR deems Barnet should raise more locally, and structural pressure for larger future council tax increases to offset this. The council states it raises less income through council tax than would be expected on a notional basis given its tax base.
findings.matters: Understanding whether the budget gap is structural or cyclical is crucial for a lender. Structural underfunding from the funding formula means the gap cannot be solved by efficiency alone and requires permanent higher council tax or central government funding changes.
findings.figures: Barnet has one of the lowest council tax rates in London and a large tax base
findings.quote: Barnet has a large tax base and has historically maintained one of the lowest council tax rates in London. We have a lower council tax yield per household than many authorities of a similar size and, as a result, Barnet raises less income through Council Tax than would be expected on a notional basis

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: New Liberata revenues contract from October 2026 targets collection rate increase to 98.93% by 2030/31, adding up to £5.9m annual income by 2031/32
findings.detail: From 1 October 2026, Liberata operates Revenues and Benefits. The contract includes progressively increasing baseline collection targets: 97.37% (2027/28), 98.39% (2028/29), 98.66% (2029/30), 98.93% (2030/31+). The council models a potential ultimate 99.0% outcome. The MTFS embeds projected improvements as additional council tax income: £3.113m (2028/29), £4.224m (2029/30), £5.480m (2030/31), £5.879m (2031/32). The council describes this as a prudent level, acknowledging opportunities and risks in a challenging economic environment.
findings.matters: This represents a concrete initiative to improve council income through operational performance. However, it is also a risk: failure to deliver means income falls short and the gap widens. The £5.9m contribution to future-year budgets makes delivery material to sustainability.
findings.quote: Contractual in-year collection targets increase progressively from 96.0% in 2027/28 to 98.0% by 2030/31, supported by enhanced debt-recovery activity and incentivised arrears collection arrangements.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Council seeking MHCLG approval for council tax increases above 2.99% referendum limit; decisions unlikely before late 2026/early 2027
findings.detail: Standard referendum limits are 2.99% general and 2.00% Adult Social Care precept. The council recognises that increases above these limits will be central to financial sustainability. Rather than hold a local referendum, it is seeking bespoke exceptional-circumstances approval from MHCLG, an approach most councils have pursued in recent years. Conversations are ongoing but decisions are unlikely until late 2026/early 2027, after the October 2026 Autumn Budget. The timing is material to December budget updates and final settlement.
findings.matters: Above-referendum flexibility would materially reduce the budget gap and demonstrate government support for the council. Refusal would leave an unfunded gap. Timing uncertainty affects budget finalization and public consultation.
findings.figures: 2.99% general, 2.00% Adult Social Care precept are standard referendum limits
findings.quote: Conversations are ongoing with MHCLG with regards to possible Council Tax increases above referendum limits but decisions are unlikely to be known until late 2026/early 2027.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability Plan targets exit from EFS by March 2029 through transformation across five themes and three enabling capabilities
findings.detail: The council has developed a Financial Sustainability Plan (FSP) structured around five themes (prevention, independence/progression, productivity, service/asset optimization, income growth) supported by three enabling capabilities (prediction, organizational capability, sound financial governance). The FSP aims to reduce demand, lower delivery costs, increase income, and end reliance on EFS by March 2029. However, opportunities from the FSP will only be incorporated into the MTFS once they have robust business cases with clearly defined financial impacts, named owner, risk assessment, and delivery milestones. The current MTFS contains no savings from the FSP, which will be added as projects are approved in future updates.
findings.matters: A lender must see evidence of a credible plan to exit structural funding dependence. The FSP provides the road map, but credibility depends on delivering specific projects with business cases. The March 2029 target is ambitious and material to the sustainability case.
findings.figures: March 2029 is the target exit date for EFS reliance
findings.quote: The FSP is being presented to this Cabinet and outlines the actions that the council is taking to achieve financial sustainability by March 2029... Together, they provide a route to reduce future demand, lower the cost of delivery, increase recurring income and end reliance on Exceptional Financial Support by March 2029.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Proposed savings of £7.9m for 2027/28 fall far short of identified pressures of £39.5m; full MTFS shows £21.2m savings against £149.1m pressures
findings.detail: Departments have identified £39.5m of spending pressures for 2027/28 (social care £11.2m, temporary accommodation/housing benefit £8.4m, EFS financing £9.6m), but propose only £7.9m of savings and income generation. Across the five-year MTFS, total pressures identified are £149.1m against proposed savings of £21.2m. The paper notes there are potential delivery risks around savings proposals, indicating these are not yet certain.
findings.matters: The 6:1 ratio of pressures to savings shows the council is not currently addressing its underlying deficit through operational efficiency. A lender assesses whether the council's savings plans are credible and proportionate to the challenge it faces.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £39.456m pressures, £7.863m savings identified; full MTFS: £149.129m total pressures, £21.204m total savings
findings.quote: Departments have identified savings of £7.9m to help plug the gap for 2027/28 as shown below... There are potential delivery risks around savings which will be managed as plans progress.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Financing costs of EFS borrowing grow from £9.6m (2027/28) to £22.6m (2030/31), forming material budget pressure
findings.detail: EFS borrowing carries revenue costs in interest and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP). These financing costs are now embedded in departmental pressures and escalate from £9.6m in 2027/28 to peak at £22.6m in 2030/31. The growing debt service reflects accumulating borrowing and represents a fixed cost that worsens the underlying deficit position.
findings.matters: EFS defers rather than solves the problem; each year's borrowing increases future-year debt service costs. A lender needs to see whether underlying operational deficits are being addressed or merely pushed forward at increasing cost.
findings.quote: The most significant pressures are being seen in both demand and costs of providing social care services, addressing homelessness, and meeting the shortfall caused by housing benefit rates that have not been updated since 2011, as well as the financing costs of EFS.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support approved up to £79.6m for 2026/27 with £73.6m drawn; approval sought for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council finances its deficit through MHCLG's Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)—government-approved borrowing. EFS was approved up to £55.7m in 2025/26 (£45.9m used) and up to £79.6m for 2026/27 (£73.6m expected to be required). The council is now seeking approval for 2027/28 EFS, with clarification on process awaited from MHCLG. The escalating approval requirement evidences deteriorating underlying finances.
findings.matters: Escalating EFS shows the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources or any realistic savings plan, and relies on central government approval to finance its operations. A lender needs to know if this dependency will end or deepen.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £55.7m approved, £45.9m used; 2026/27: £79.6m approved in principle, £73.6m expected required
findings.quote: MHCLG approved Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of up to £55.7m in 2025/26, of which only £45.9m was required; and has approved in principle EFS of up to £79.6m for 2026/27 of which £73.6m is expected to be required

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2027-2032 (Medium Term Financial Strategy)
findings.headline: Budget gap of £113.5m identified for 2027/28, widening to £228.2m by 2031/32 across the five-year MTFS
findings.detail: The council faces a significant and deteriorating budget position, with deficits growing from £113.5m in 2027/28 to £144.1m (2028/29), £183.7m (2029/30), £220.5m (2030/31), and £228.2m (2031/32). These represent the scale of savings or external funding needed to achieve balance each year before any mitigation.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council has an underlying structural deficit that will persist or a temporary funding gap. The trajectory and scale determine whether external support is sustainable.
findings.quote: there remains a budget gap is £113.5m for 2027/28

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council establishing dedicated Financial Sustainability Delivery Team to manage programme implementation with quarterly Cabinet reporting
findings.detail: Delivery of the plan will be supported by a dedicated Financial Sustainability Delivery Team formed primarily through secondment and redeployment of existing council capacity. The team will support delivery of the in-flight opportunities, develop the pipeline, manage the investment process, and handle benefits realisation. Progress, risks, and delivery against financial targets will be monitored through quarterly Cabinet updates with named Chief Officer and Cabinet lead ownership for each opportunity.
findings.matters: Shows council is committing dedicated resource to delivery; quarterly reporting to Cabinet provides visibility of progress; named ownership creates accountability for delivery.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Delivery of the Plan will be supported by a dedicated Financial Sustainability Delivery Team, formed primarily through secondment and redeployment of existing capacity.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council planning asset disposal programme and capital cost reduction as part of Service and Asset Review
findings.detail: The Service and Asset Review workstream includes a programme of work to reduce capital and financing costs, development of a Strategic Asset Management Plan, and a programme of asset disposals. This is aimed at both reducing capital spend and reducing ongoing financing costs from the council's asset base.
findings.matters: Signals council intends to deploy asset sales and rationalization as part of financial recovery; relevant to lenders assessing asset base, liquidity, and collateral position.
findings.figures: No specific disposal targets stated
findings.quote: The Plan includes a Service and Asset Review focussed on how the Council's services and assets can best support service delivery, financial sustainability and value for money. This includes a programme of work to reduce capital and financing costs, alongside the development of a Strategic Asset Management Plan and a programme of asset disposals.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council states financial sustainability cannot be achieved through income increases alone and requires reduction in expenditure growth rate
findings.detail: While additional income including Council Tax increases forms part of the council's response, the council explicitly states that lasting sustainability requires both recurring income and a reduction in the growth rate of expenditure. This signals that the council has limited headroom to raise further income and that the sustainability challenge must be addressed primarily through spending control and service model change.
findings.matters: Indicates the council's view that it cannot tax its way out of this challenge; demonstrates recognition that structural cost control is necessary and that there are limits to income-raising capacity.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Additional income, including Council Tax, forms part of the Council's response, but financial sustainability cannot be achieved through income alone. Lasting sustainability requires both recurring income and a reduction in the growth rate of expenditure.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council forecasts that cost growth and demand pressures will continue to rise, with deficit expected to grow further despite planned interventions
findings.detail: Budget modelling indicates that need and costs are due to rise further beyond initial forecasts, and the deficit is projected to grow again. This means the council cannot rely on baseline cost controls; it requires the transformation programme to outpace underlying demand and cost growth. The council will need to continue developing and testing opportunities through the pipeline to address this ongoing pressure.
findings.matters: Shows that cost pressures are structural and ongoing, not temporary; single-round interventions will not solve this; continuing management capacity is required.
findings.figures: Deficit projected to grow again
findings.quote: However, budget modelling and forecasting work has illustrated that need and costs are due to rise further and the deficit is projected to grow again.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Barnet sets £200m target for financial benefits needed by 2029/2030 to achieve sustainability and end reliance on Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council has set a total target of £200m in financial benefits needed to make the council financially sustainable by 2029/30. This exceeds the £198m forecast gap to provide buffer for forecast changes and to specifically help end reliance on Exceptional Financial Support. The plan will be refreshed as delivery progresses and forecasts are refined.
findings.matters: Sets the scale of three-year transformation programme required; indicates council's assessment of what is necessary and sufficient to restore financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £200m target by 2029/30; exceeds £198m forecast gap
findings.quote: The £200m target is based on the forecast budget gap and reflects the financial benefits needed to make the council financially sustainable by 2029/30.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council has identified £84m of additional savings opportunities in first wave of delivery portfolio to meet immediate budget challenge
findings.detail: The Plan has identified £84m of additional opportunities currently in-flight for development and delivery, beyond savings already secured in existing financial plans. The council states this scale of innovation meets the quantum of the 2026/27 budget gap. Each opportunity has a named Chief Officer and Cabinet lead with quarterly progress reporting to Cabinet.
findings.matters: Shows what immediate savings the council believes it can deliver and provides early evidence of programme implementation; first concrete step toward addressing the structural deficit.
findings.figures: £84m identified in Wave 1 portfolio; stated to meet 2026/27 budget gap quantum
findings.quote: The Plan has identified £84m of additional opportunities to meet the budget challenge, in addition to the savings already secured in existing financial plans.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: OPFS Cabinet report
findings.headline: Barnet Council forecasts structural budget gap of £198m by 2029/2030 with expenditure growing faster than available income
findings.detail: The council faces a significant structural financial challenge with expenditure forecast to grow faster than available income, resulting in a projected budget gap of £198m by 2029/2030. This has resulted in continued reliance on Exceptional Financial Support. The Financial Sustainability Plan is the council's response to this challenge.
findings.matters: A forecast structural deficit of this scale indicates severe underlying financial pressures; councils do not receive Exceptional Financial Support without demonstrating genuine distress.
findings.figures: £198m deficit forecast by 2029/2030
findings.quote: Expenditure is forecast to grow faster than available income, resulting in a forecast budget gap of £198m by 2029/2030 and continued reliance on Exceptional Financial Support without further intervention.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Partnership library agreements require £65k uplift in 2027/28, including transition of Childs Hill Library to direct operation
findings.detail: Four partnership libraries under grant agreements expire 31 March 2027. Two partners will extend for 12 months with grant uplifts of £43k. A third partner (Kisharon Langdon - Childs Hill Library) will conclude its agreement; the library will return to direct council operation, requiring operational budget of £21.5k net of the withdrawn grant and identified efficiencies.
findings.matters: This shows a shift from partnership delivery to direct council operation of a library service, with associated cost and workforce implications, and signals a review of the wider library service is underway.
findings.figures: Partner grant uplifts £43,417; Childs Hill transition net cost £21,583; combined pressure £65,000 (one-off 2027/28)
findings.quote: The combined Growth Pressure requirement is therefore £65,000 which is intended as a one off pressure for 27/28 with a wider project initiated to review the future of the library service.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Fleet replacement programme delayed by Better Barnet Recycling uncertainty, requiring temporary vehicle leasing
findings.detail: Delays in agreeing the future of the 'Better Barnet Recycling' programme have delayed the Fleet Replacement programme. The council must lease additional vehicles to replace the most uneconomical RCVs (approximately 10) and keep existing vehicles longer than planned, which may incur extra maintenance costs in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that a capital programme delay is creating short-term revenue costs (leasing and maintenance) instead of capital expenditure, and that the delay is tied to uncertainty in a major service transformation project.
findings.quote: As a result of potential delays in agreeing the future of 'Better Barnet Recycling' programme,which will delay the Fleet Replacement programme. Therefore, there is a need to lease a number of additional vehicles to replace the most uneconomical RCVs - approx 10 - and keep existing vehicles for longer than planned which may incur extra maintenance costs in 28/29.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Local election reserve projected to fall short of 2030 election costs by £806k
findings.detail: The 2026 local election cost £1,100,303 against a reserve of £916k, creating a £184k shortfall. The council budgets £178k annually into the election reserve. By 2029/30, the projected reserve will total £534k, but the estimated cost of the 2030 local election is £1.34m, creating a shortfall of £806k that will need to be funded.
findings.matters: Election costs are one-time demands the council cannot avoid; growing shortfalls suggest either election costs are rising faster than anticipated or reserve contributions are insufficient.
findings.figures: 2026 election cost £1,100,303; reserve available £916k; shortfall £184k; 2030 election projected cost £1.34m; projected reserve £534k; pressure £806k in 2029/30
findings.quote: The cost of 2026 local election was £1,100,303, with the reserve available to cover is £916k leaving a short fall of £184k... The current projected cost of the Local Election in 2030 is £1.34m - leaving a shortfall (pressure) of £806k in 29/30.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Governance restructuring following May 2026 elections adding £220k in 2027/28 for additional scrutiny and opposition support staffing
findings.detail: Following the May 2026 elections and 'no overall control' council agreement, governance changes include two new Scrutiny Committees, reinstatement of three Area Committees, and reduction of Planning Committees to one. These changes require new posts: an additional Strategic Advisor for the Opposition Group and an additional Governance and Scrutiny Officer.
findings.matters: A governance restructuring creates permanent new cost commitments; this shows the council's political structure and associated costs changing following the election.
findings.quote: As per 'no overall control' agreement post May 2026 Elections, Governance Services changes including two new Scrutiny Committees, reinstate three Areas Committees, reduction of Planning Committees to one Planning Committee as per legislation, funding of additional Member Pension budget. In addition, creation of an additional Strategic Advisor for the Opposition Group (Grade L) and additional Governance and Scrutiny Officer (Grade I) to support the new committees.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Local Plan Review accelerated with statutory obligation requiring evidence-base preparation from September 2026 and adoption targeted for 2029
findings.detail: The council faces a statutory obligation to review its Local Plan. Following publication of the draft London Plan, the council is planning an accelerated programme with pre-commencement work from September 2026, Gateway 1 from late 2026, and adoption targeted for 2029. This work is resource and evidence-intensive, requiring external support for specialist studies, legal/planning inspectorate support, consultation and examination.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council faces a significant resource and cost commitment to meet statutory planning obligations; this is a mandated spend that affects available resources for other priorities.
findings.figures: Bid £510k over 5 years (155k, 305k, 100k, -50k for periods 2027-2031)
findings.quote: The Council has a statutory obligation to review its Local Plan. Recent internal discussions following publication of draft London Plan identify a need to consider an accelerated programme, with pre-commencement evidence-base work beginning from September 2026 and Gateway 1 / notice of intention to commence plan preparation from as early as late 2026.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Building Safety Act compliance requiring new processes and bi-annual regulator audits, with audit cost circa £1k per day
findings.detail: The Building Safety Regulator requires building control services to deposit monitoring arrangements reports bi-annually and will audit these reports over a period of one to two months. The council must cover the cost of these audits. The service also requires rebranding and new KPI reporting to promote its new role as Registered Building Inspectors.
findings.matters: This is a new regulatory compliance requirement that creates an ongoing cost burden. The daily audit cost creates a material expense for services already under pressure.
findings.figures: Pressure shown as £55k in some years with bi-annual variation
findings.quote: Legislation dictates that building control bodies, such as the Council, will then have to cover the cost of the BSR to do so - circa £1k per day.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Income lost from Local Land Charges searches following government's mandatory transfer of function to HM Land Registry
findings.detail: Government policy centralizes Local Land Charges searches at HM Land Registry. This removes the council's ability to charge for these searches and generates no replacement funding. The council faces an ongoing income loss as a result.
findings.matters: This is a direct loss of a revenue income stream created by government policy, with no compensation — it exemplifies councils' exposure to government policy changes over income sources.
findings.figures: Loss creates ongoing income challenge; specific quantum shown in pressures
findings.quote: As Local Land Charges 1 searches are handed over to HM Land Registry. , local authorities lose the ability to charge for these searches, leading to a significant reduction in income that is not replaced by alternative funding.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: SEND legal spending pressure of £287k becomes permanent after Early Years DSG top-slice flexibility withdrawn by DfE
findings.detail: Legal spend on education, particularly EHCP advice and tribunal representation, has grown from £372k budget to forecast spend of £657k in 2026/27. This pressure was previously offset by flexibility in the Early Years block top-slice, but the DfE's new minimum pass-through rate requirement removes that mitigation. The top-slice fell from £556k to £161k, making the legal spend a permanent pressure.
findings.matters: This shows a shift in funding risk from the council's discretionary control to a structural deficit created by DfE policy changes — a pressure that cannot be internally managed.
findings.quote: This has been an on-going pressure but has been able to be mitigated against by increases in the Early Years top-slice. In 2025/26 this pressure was able to be offset by a large top-slice from the Early Years block of the DSG of £556,877, however in 2026/27 this top-slice was only £161k due to increases in the minimum pass-through rate imposed by the DfE.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand pressures from demographic growth and complexity growing from £3.9m to £8.4m annually
findings.detail: Adult Social Care faces ongoing demand growth driven by demographic changes and increasing complexity of cases. The annual pressure grows from £3,940k in 2027/28 to £8,362k by 2031/32. Additionally, the council faces £13.6m in provider inflation costs across the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Demographic pressures on social care are a major structural issue for councils; a doubling of annual pressure within 5 years indicates the council faces significant service and funding challenges.
findings.quote: Demographic growth and increase in complexity

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy shortfall growing from £1.9m to £2.1m as temporary accommodation claims exceed reimbursable subsidy
findings.detail: The council faces a gap between housing benefit paid out and the amount it can claim back in subsidy. The largest component relates to temporary accommodation; supported accommodation and overpayments also contribute. The pressure grows from £1,892k in 2027/28 to £2,139k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: This represents a structural funding gap the council must cover from its own resources, tied directly to its temporary accommodation pressures and government subsidy rules.
findings.quote: This pressure relates to the gap between HB paid out and subsidy we are permitted to claim. The largest gap relates to Temp Accommodation but supported accommodation and overpayments also result in gaps.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Net temporary accommodation costs increasing, driven by higher emergency accommodation prices and growing demand
findings.detail: TA costs are growing from a combination of increased demand for accommodation and rises in the costs of nightly-paid emergency accommodation. The council reports that accommodation prices are increasing with each renewal. This is happening alongside broader housing demand pressures.
findings.matters: TA is a major and persistent cost pressure for councils; growth driven by both demand and price inflation indicates the council will struggle to manage this without intervention or increased funding.
findings.figures: TA net costs 2027/28 £5,648k; 2028/29 £6,907k; 2029/30 £6,602k; total TA-related pressures £30,942k across 5 years
findings.quote: The net cost of TA (Temporary Accommodation costs less rental income) has increased due to demand and higher nightly paid emergency accommodation. Overall accommodation prices have increased so each renewal is at a higher rate.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Service Pressures
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support financing costs to grow from £9.6m in 2027/28 to £22.6m in 2030/31
findings.detail: The council faces £62.75m in Exceptional Financial Support financing costs across the MTFS period, with costs more than doubling from 2027/28 to 2030/31 before dropping to zero in 2031/32. This represents a major financing burden that will peak in 2030/31.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's borrowing trajectory and what is driving the escalating financing costs, which could indicate growing reliance on exceptional financial support or rising rates.
findings.quote: Financing costs relating to Exceptional Financial Support Financing Costs

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: Only £18m of £544m (3.3%) of 2026/27 budget is genuinely discretionary spending; council must achieve savings through efficiency and demand management rather than service cuts
findings.detail: Council examined how much of spending is truly discretionary. Excluding activity funded entirely by others, only £18m is spent on services the council is not legally required to provide or which are not otherwise essential. Most budget is committed to statutory services.
findings.matters: Explains structural constraints on council's flexibility; financial sustainability cannot be achieved through discretionary cuts alone, requiring demand management and efficiency improvement across mandatory services
findings.figures: £18m discretionary of £544m total budget (3.3%); remaining £526m committed or essential
findings.quote: Excluding activity funded entirely by others, only around £18m of the Council's £544m budget in 2026/27 is spent on services it is not required to provide, or which are not otherwise essential.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: £116m of £200m target sits in development pipeline; pipeline deliberately sized to exceed requirement to provide resilience against non-delivery
findings.detail: Council has identified £84m of opportunities and estimates £116m-£165m in further pipeline opportunities to reach £200m target. Council acknowledges delivery risk and has sized pipeline above the minimum required to provide buffer for non-delivery. Plan includes £5m annual contingency and assumes 15% of planned savings will not be delivered.
findings.matters: Large proportion of financial plan depends on unproven opportunities; council's assessment of delivery resilience will determine whether variance in outcomes occurs within or outside contingency buffer
findings.figures: £116m from pipeline of £200m total; £84m identified opportunities; £120m-£165m pipeline range; £5m annual contingency; 15% non-delivery assumption
findings.quote: The remaining £116m represents the remaining delivery requirement to close the projected gap... The pipeline deliberately exceeds the remaining requirement to provide resilience against non-delivery.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: Adult social care costs reduced below national average while maintaining top-quartile performance, but social care need and complexity forecast to rise by £32m through 2029/30
findings.detail: Council has achieved both cost control and quality: costs are below the national average while performance remains in top quartile. Council has also stabilised temporary accommodation spending through prevention work. However, forecast shows social care need and complexity continuing to rise materially, offsetting cost management gains.
findings.matters: Shows council has some levers for cost control but suggests structural demand growth may outpace efficiency efforts; key indicator of medium-term financial sustainability challenge for comparable councils
findings.figures: Costs below national average; top-quartile performance maintained; £32m social care cost growth projected by 2029/30
findings.quote: Since 2024/2025 (the year from which data considered by the 2026 CIPFA review was drawn) the council has reduced adult social care costs below the national average per adult while maintaining top-quartile performance, and stabilised in-year temporary accommodation spending, through a programme of work with the Barnet Group to prevent homelessness to avoid placements in Temporary Accommodation as well as moving residents out of Temporary Accommodation.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: "Reduced independence" accounts for £90m (40%) of statutory spending across three service areas but received less than £1.5m of £23.1m prevention expenditure
findings.detail: Cost-driver analysis of £230.4m of statutory expenditure across adult social care, children's services and temporary accommodation identified 13 major drivers. Reduced independence—residents becoming less able to manage daily life without support—is by far the largest, accounting for 40% of total and twice the size of the next largest driver. Yet prevention spending is not well aligned: reduced independence was only the fourth largest focus and received minimal funding relative to its impact.
findings.matters: Suggests council understands root causes of cost growth but current spending allocation does not reflect those causes; identifies potential for more efficient resource targeting and reallocation
findings.figures: £90m for reduced independence; approximately 40% of £230.4m total analysed; £23.1m total prevention expenditure; less than £1.5m on reduced independence prevention
findings.quote: The largest driver was reduced independence – that is residents becoming less able to manage daily life without support. It accounted for around £90m of expenditure, approximately 40% of the total analysed and more than twice the size of the next largest driver. Reduced independence was only the fourth largest focus of prevention spending and received less than £1.5m of the £23.1m of prevention expenditure identified.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: Council delivered 95.8% of planned savings in 2025/26 and used £10m less Exceptional Financial Support than government approved
findings.detail: Council has strengthened financial controls since 2024, rebuilt budget on realistic basis, and improved forecasting accuracy through tighter control of spending, recruitment and agency costs. Delivery track record shows council can execute on financial plans and is outperforming approved EFS allocation.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council has capability to deliver on complex financial targets; peer councils and lenders need evidence of execution track record before assessing credibility of larger transformation plan
findings.figures: 95.8% planned savings delivery rate; £10m EFS underspend; controls in place since 2024
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council delivered 95.8% of planned savings, delivered within its agreed budget and used approximately £10m less Exceptional Financial Support than had been approved by Government.

findings.committee: Cabinet

findings.detail: Council has identified £84m of opportunities to contribute to the £200m target, but £71m comes from modelled Council Tax increase requiring approval from both Secretary of State and elected members. Remaining £116m to reach the £200m target sits in development pipeline. Government funding assumption is based on Band D charge of £2,060, but Barnet currently charges £1,622.
findings.matters: Council's ability to meet plan depends on decisions it cannot make unilaterally and on unproven opportunities in development pipeline; represents significant implementation and approval risk

findings.quote: A significant proportion of the £84m identified relates to Council Tax reflecting the current relative early stage of the portfolio's development... This has not yet been approved and would require agreement from the Secretary of State and elected members.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: Council will require continued government Exceptional Financial Support through 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29 to cover budget shortfalls
findings.detail: Council received Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26 because it could not balance its budget from own resources. The plan projects EFS will remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29, with £40m of the projected cost growth by 2029/30 accounted for by financing costs of support already received.
findings.matters: EFS is government-approved borrowing; its financing costs accumulate and place additional pressure on future budgets regardless of other council actions, constraining financial flexibility
findings.figures: EFS received 2025/26; £40m financing cost impact by 2029/30; EFS likely needed 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29
findings.quote: The Council therefore needed the Government's permission to meet costs from borrowing and the sale of assets, called Exceptional Financial Support. This support must be repaid and gives rise to ongoing financing costs that place additional pressure on future budgets... On any realistic profile, Exceptional Financial Support is likely to remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Annex A - Our Plan for Financial Sustainability 2026-29
findings.headline: Budget gap forecast to grow from £79.3m in 2026/27 to £198m in 2029/30, driven by rising demand for adult social care, temporary accommodation and children's services outpacing income growth
findings.detail: Expenditure is forecast to rise £209m over three years while income rises only £83m, deteriorating financial position by roughly £40m a year. The increase reflects combined effect of rising demand, increasing complexity of need, inflation and financing costs.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand the scale and nature of the structural pressure and whether savings plans address root causes or merely manage symptoms
findings.figures: £79.3m gap 2026/27; £198m gap 2029/30; £209m expenditure growth over three years; £83m income growth over three years; £40m deterioration per year
findings.quote: Spending, overwhelmingly on statutory services that the council has to provide, is growing faster than the resources available to fund it, and without further action the gap is forecast to increase significantly over the medium term.

findings.committee: Cabinet

findings.detail: Service & Asset Review workstream includes capital programme review (Stage 2, moving to next phase Q3 2026-27) to reduce borrowing requirements and future financing costs, and Strategic Asset Management Plan to identify disposals and generate capital receipts to lower borrowing. Both targeted to yield £250k–£1m benefit.

Prevention and Progression initiatives face risks including benefits representing avoided costs, longer payback periods, and impacts being difficult to attribute.

Service efficiency initiatives in early stages with avoided-cost models carry higher risk of non-realization than direct operational savings.

findings.detail: Portfolio includes council tax review modelling net recurring income after the Council Tax Reduction Scheme, accounting for £70m of the ~£82.5m total portfolio benefit. The workstream requires progression through Cabinet and Full Council decisions expected October-December 2026.
findings.matters: Council tax decisions fundamentally affect both the council's financial position and residents' affordability. With £70m of an £82.5m portfolio dependent on this income, the council's recovery plan is substantially reliant on tax increase approval.

findings.detail: RSG falls from £58.8m in 2026/27 to £18.5m in 2027/28 (£40.3m loss in one year), then continues declining to zero by 2031/32. The council faces a planned, multi-year withdrawal of a core funding stream.

findings.detail: Total government grants are £37.7m in 2026/27, drop to £11.9m in 2027/28, and fall to £0.000 from 2028/29. The Social Care Grant of £31.8m, Children and families grant of £4.1m, and other grants end after 2026/27. This £37.7m cliff coincides with the start of unresolved deficits.

The paper shows no contribution to or drawdown from reserves in those years, leaving these deficits unresolved.

findings.headline: Budget gap of £113.5m for 2027/28, growing to £228.2m by 2031/32 despite identified savings

findings.committee: Finance and Growth Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix D - CIPFA financial management assessment
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability Plan with cost-driver-led approach targeting financial sustainability by March 2029
findings.detail: The council has developed a Financial Sustainability Plan to be presented to Cabinet in October 2026, shifting from reactive budget management to demand-side intervention. The plan focuses on prevention (identifying and tackling root causes of demand in high-cost services using predictive analytics) and working smarter (reducing avoidable demand and duplication). It includes five delivery blocks and three enabling blocks with governance and benefits realisation arrangements.
findings.matters: Represents strategic shift toward structural reform rather than incremental savings; public timeline to sustainability (March 2029) is important for lenders and peer councils assessing recovery trajectory and commitment.
findings.figures: March 2029 sustainability target, five delivery blocks, three enabling blocks
findings.quote: The council has a target to become a financially sustainable council by March 2029... The council's Financial Sustainability Plan (FSP) is being presented to Cabinet in October 2026. The FSP introduces a cost-driver-led approach to financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Only 55% of audit actions were implemented by deadline in Q1, against a target of 90%
findings.detail: The council is systematically failing to implement high-priority audit recommendations on time. This significantly misses the 90% target and the 2025/26 full-year implementation rate of 74%, representing a persistent control environment weakness that the Head of Internal Audit has flagged as material to the annual conclusion.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council can identify and remedy control weaknesses; systematic failure to implement audit recommendations suggests the organisation cannot act on its own findings, which is a material control risk.

findings.quote: In total, 55% of actions followed up in Q1 were confirmed as implemented. This remains significantly below the Council's target of 90% and is also below the 2025/26 full-year implementation rate of 74%.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment valuation adjustment of £1.495m identified due to late receipt of fund manager confirmations
findings.detail: During audit testing of Level 3 investments, a £1.495m difference was found between the value recorded in the draft financial statements and the value confirmed by fund managers. Management agreed to update the accounts. The difference arose because the fund manager's valuation was not available when the draft accounts were initially prepared, representing a timing issue rather than a management error.
findings.matters: While characterized as a timing issue, it shows that investment values in the pension fund accounts are not immediately confirmed at year end, creating a lag in the accuracy of reported pension fund assets. This affects the reliability of funding position assessments.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Member data processing is delayed, with joiners not admitted to the fund until the following year
findings.detail: During testing, auditors identified one member who completed starter documentation in 2024-25 but was not admitted to the fund until 2025-26. This triggered an extension of testing from 25 to 50 member records. While no further exceptions were found in the extended testing, the auditor concluded the exception represented an 'isolated control deficiency'. The recommendation is for management to strengthen oversight controls with the external administrator and reconcile completed starter documentation against members actually admitted.
findings.matters: Processing delays affect the completeness and accuracy of member data used to calculate pension liabilities and employer contribution rates. Delayed admissions mean contributions may be recorded in the wrong financial period, understating pension liabilities in the year of joining.
findings.figures: 1 delayed admission identified; extended testing to 50 from 25 samples

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation process has material control weaknesses with £562k unreconciled from a partner pension fund
findings.detail: The fund holds a £841k receivable from West Yorkshire Pension Fund with £562k remaining unreconciled at year end. Separately, the audit found that a £2.1m cash-in-transit balance recorded in the general ledger was not included in the reconciliation, and an £8k USD account balance plus in-year transactions were completely omitted from both the general ledger and reconciliation. These errors were only caught during the audit.
findings.matters: Cash and bank balances are inherently fraud-sensitive and require strong controls. Material gaps in reconciliation processes indicate broader financial control weaknesses in the pension fund administration. As the council is the administering authority, these weaknesses reflect on the council's financial management.
findings.figures: £562k unreconciled; £2.1m cash-in-transit omitted; £8k USD balance omitted

findings.headline: Fund contributions now fall short of benefit payments, creating structural operating deficit
findings.detail: Benefits paid (£81.2mn) now exceed member contributions (£76.3mn) by approximately £4.9mn per annum, a structural change reflecting fund maturity. The council states this deficit is offset by investment income under the fund's income-generating investment strategy.
findings.matters: This represents a fundamental shift in the fund's financial structure from contribution-driven to investment-return-dependent, creating exposure to investment market volatility that could necessitate increased employer contributions to the fund if returns fall.
findings.figures: Member contributions £76.3mn (+3.9%), member benefits £81.2mn (+6.2%), investment returns £137.8mn (including £35.6mn income)
findings.quote: Contributions increased by 3.9% from £73.4mn to £76.3mn, while benefits increased by 6.2% from £76.4mn to £81.2mn. The greater increase in benefits compared to contributions reflects the increasing maturity of the Fund and is in line with most other LGPS funds. As a consequence the Fund is now cashflow negative on an operational basis. This negative cashflow is more than compensated by investment income derived by the Fund's strategy to invest in income generating investments.

findings.matters: Service investment lending introduces counterparty and credit risk to the balance sheet. Large loans to regeneration vehicles or sports entities can default. The council's caution here suggests concern about repayment security.
