findings.quote: This is due to the high risk and high value nature of most current and future loans to third parties, and the potential volatility of the ECL calculation.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Treasury Management Strategy (TMSS) 26-27
findings.headline: The council is using a Capitalisation Direction to borrow £55.7m to treat revenue expenditure as capital, indicating pressure on the revenue budget.
findings.detail: In 2025/26, the council applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to use a Capitalisation Direction, allowing it to treat specified revenue costs as capital expenditure and fund them through borrowing instead of the revenue budget. This is a formal mechanism for dealing with unaffordable revenue pressures.
findings.matters: Use of capitalisation directions signals underlying revenue budget pressure that cannot be accommodated within normal spending. While permitted by government, it defers costs and adds borrowing. Lenders should understand what revenue pressures exist.
findings.figures: £55.7m of revenue expenditure being capitalised and financed by borrowing in 2025/26.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the council intends to borrow up to £55.7m as part of the EFS application to apply the Capitalisation Direction. This allows local authorities to treat certain types of revenue expenditure as capital expenditure, allowing them to be funded by borrowing or capital receipts as opposed to from the revenue budget.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Treasury Management Strategy (TMSS) 26-27
findings.headline: Council reserves have depleted from prior surpluses to a minimum liquidity buffer of £50m and will remain at that level.
findings.detail: The council's excess cash reserves, which provided a financial cushion in prior years, have been used down. The Liability Benchmark analysis confirms that excess cash levels have reduced to the council's defined liquidity buffer (£50m) and will remain constrained at that level through 2026/27, leaving little flexibility for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility. A thin liquidity buffer increases vulnerability to unforeseen pressures and limits ability to absorb volatility.
findings.figures: Liquidity buffer set at £50m (a £5m uplift from prior threshold); council maintaining only this level of cash over the forecast period.
findings.quote: The Liability Benchmark indicates that the council's excess cash levels, which it enjoyed over the last few years have reduced to its Liquidity Buffer and will remain around this level over 2026/27.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Treasury Management Strategy (TMSS) 26-27
findings.headline: The HRA faces significant interest rate refinancing risk as debt is expected to be held indefinitely and grow with no reduction mechanism.
findings.detail: Because the HRA housing stock and associated debt are assumed to be permanent, the council will face long-term exposure to interest rate movements when refinancing debt. As rates fluctuate, refinancing costs will vary. The council explicitly identifies this as a material risk requiring medium-term strategic consideration.
findings.matters: Interest rate exposure on growing permanent debt is a key credit risk. If rates remain elevated, HRA costs will rise further, exacerbating the rental income deficit.
findings.figures: HRA debt growing to £626.9m by 2028/29 with no planned reduction; debt per dwelling reaching £69,236.
findings.quote: This means that the HRA is exposed to increasing and significant interest rate risk (i.e., around re-financing its debt portfolio and taking on more debt).

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Treasury Management Strategy (TMSS) 26-27
findings.headline: HRA rental income is insufficient to cover all operational costs including fire safety improvements and maintenance, creating a structural deficit.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that rental income within the Housing Revenue Account does not cover property management, repair costs, major works (kitchens, bathrooms, roofs), or debt interest. This is attributed to post-Grenfell fire safety legislation, ageing housing stock, and costs rising faster than rental income. The HRA is assumed to be held in perpetuity, meaning this is an ongoing challenge.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether rental income can sustain the HRA's debt and maintenance obligations. A structural revenue deficit in housing suggests either rental increases, subsidy from the general fund, or service cuts.
findings.figures: HRA debt rising from £477.8m (2024/25) to £626.9m (2028/29); HRA debt per dwelling rising from £52,486 to £69,236; HRA debt-to-revenues ratio worsening from 622% to 690%.
findings.quote: Currently, rental income within the HRA is insufficient to pay for all property management, repair costs, major works costs (such as replacing kitchens, bathrooms, roofs etc.) and service debt interest.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Two major capital projects (£302m combined) remain only at enabling/grant-approval stage despite urgent need
findings.detail: The Depot project is estimated at ~£176m and the SEN school project at ~£126m. The council states 'further work is required before adding these to the capital programme and therefore at this stage only grant monies or enabling works monies have been included.' Both services face escalating pressures (Children's Social Care £4.354m, Communities/Adults £8.422m), yet the capital solutions remain distant.
findings.matters: These delays signal either funding uncertainty or internal delivery capacity problems. Meanwhile, revenue pressures in these areas mount. If projects slip further, capital-funded solutions that could help with demand will be delayed.
findings.figures: Depot project estimate: ~£176m; SEN school estimate: ~£126m; current stage: enabling works/grant approval only; combined service pressures 2026/27: £12.776m
findings.quote: There are two major projects where further borrowing will be required: these are the Depot project and the SEN school project. The estimate for the Depot project is in the region of £176m and the estimate for the SEN school is in the region of £126m. Further work is required before adding these to the capital programme.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Food waste collection mandate must be implemented by March 2026 with ~£3.1m annual cost but no government funding announced
findings.detail: All councils in England must provide separate weekly food waste collections by March 2026. Barnet estimates revenue costs of ~£3.1m per year. However, 'revenue funding allocations for this additional service have not yet been announced' and 'no assumptions have been made on grant funding for this service.' The unfunded cost is embedded in the pressures.
findings.matters: This is a known unfunded mandate with tight timescale. If government funding is lower than estimated, or delayed, the council will face an unplanned cost with no time to absorb it through savings.
findings.figures: Estimated annual cost: ~£3.1m; funding announced: £0; deadline: March 2026
findings.quote: By March 2026 all councils in England must provide separate weekly food waste collections. Revenue funding allocations for this additional service have not yet been announced but there is a risk that funding will not be sufficient to cover costs.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer states reserves are 'unsustainably low' and 'offer little capacity to absorb financial shocks'
findings.detail: The Executive Director of Finance explicitly assesses that 'the council's reserves position remains unsustainably low and continues to pose a risk to the council's resilience.' General Fund balances are at the minimum statutory level (£15m) and 'offer little capacity to absorb financial shocks.' Earmarked reserves have been drawn down over multiple years. The S151 recommends rebuilding reserves to a minimum of £40m 'once the council is financially sustainable,' acknowledging this cannot happen while in EFS.
findings.matters: A finance director's explicit statement that reserves are inadequate is a red flag. It means the council has no cushion for unexpected costs. Combined with the uncertain equal pay claim and developer contribution collapse, this is a stability risk.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve: £15m (minimum statutory level); earmarked reserves: £50.4m at end 2025/26; target: £40m minimum once sustainable
findings.quote: In my professional opinion, the council's reserves position remains unsustainably low and continues to pose a risk to the council's resilience. General Fund balances remain at the statutory minimum level and offer little capacity to absorb financial shocks.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: General Fund capital receipts shortfall: council plans to use £72m but only holds £55m
findings.detail: The revised capital programme assumes £72.079m will be funded from General Fund capital receipts. Current receipts stand at £55.405m. The disposal programme estimates only £0.609m in 2025/26 and £11.3m in 2026/27. The council states 'assuming no further General Fund disposals there could be a shortfall of capital receipts in future years which would be replaced by borrowing and result in additional interest and MRP costs.'
findings.matters: This is a near-term cash problem. If the council cannot generate the planned capital disposals, it will need to borrow more, adding revenue cost just when it is already in EFS. Asset sales are discretionary and may be delayed.
findings.figures: Capital receipts needed: £72.079m; receipts available: £55.405m; estimated shortfall: ~£17m; planned disposals 2026/27: £11.3m only
findings.quote: Current receipts are standing at £55.405m... Assuming no further General Fund disposals there could be a shortfall of capital receipts in future years which would be replaced by borrowing and result in additional interest and MRP costs.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate revised downward from 98% to 97.37%, reducing expected income
findings.detail: Following a review of data from the council's billing service provider, the assumed 4-year collection rate was revised down. The council identified two calculation issues: credit balances were not excluded and payments subsequently transferred to other years were not reflected. Capita calculated the actual rate at 97.07% as at March 2025, with 97.37% assumed for 2026/27. The council is working on credit balance write-backs but these will not impact the Collection Fund until 2027/28.
findings.matters: Collection rate assumptions are opaque to external readers and vulnerable to hidden collection problems. A downward revision signals actual performance is worse than previously stated. The timing lag (2027/28 for credit balance impact) means this remains a risk.
findings.figures: Previous assumption: 98%; revised to 97.37%; underlying rate calculated at 97.07% as at March 2025
findings.quote: Following a review of the information provided by Capita, a number of issues were identified in the calculation of the 4-year collection rate... Both of these over-stated the 4-year collection rate.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs have seen unprecedented increases over two years with no end in sight
findings.detail: TA is the single largest pressure, at £11.3m in 2026/27 alone. The council attributes this to 'demand and higher nightly paid emergency accommodation' and notes that 'overall accommodation prices have increased so each renewal is at a higher rate.' Pressures are modelled to continue through 2030/31 (£3.954m that year). The council has identified TA reduction as a strategic priority but savings proposals are modest (£2.8m in 2026/27).
findings.matters: Homelessness and TA costs are increasingly difficult for councils to control. A lender needs to understand whether this council has a credible strategy to bend this demand curve, or whether it will continue absorbing these costs.
findings.figures: £11.305m pressure 2026/27; cumulative 5-year pressure £27.165m through 2030/31; £2.8m identified savings in 2026/27 only
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation costs have seen an unprecedented increase over the last two years. The net cost of TA (i.e. TA costs less rental income) has increased due to demand and higher nightly paid emergency accommodation.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit continues to grow beyond 2026/27, reaching £243.5m by 2031 even with EFS
findings.detail: The MTFS shows the budget gap continues to increase year-on-year after 2026/27. By 2030/31 the unfunded gap is £243.5m, with EFS financing costs alone reaching £22.6m. The council explicitly states EFS 'is not, and is not intended to be, a long-term solution' and acknowledges it faces 'a significant hill to climb in order to get back to financial sustainability.'
findings.matters: The trend suggests Barnet has not addressed underlying drivers of its financial problems. Lenders need to know whether a council's financial distress is temporary or structural.
findings.quote: The MTFS shows the budget gap increasing across the MTFS period due to cost pressures with a forecast budget gap of £244m in 2031.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Business Planning 2026-2031 (Medium Term Financial Strategy) March 26 Council
findings.headline: Council cannot balance 2026/27 budget without £79.6m capitalisation direction from government
findings.detail: Despite identifying £9.4m of savings, the council faces a £79.3m unfunded gap. Government approval of Exceptional Financial Support (a capitalisation direction) is conditional on external assurance review. The council can borrow to fund revenue costs only under this direction. Any borrowing incurs interest and Minimum Revenue Provision costs, adding £6.7m to 2026/27 pressures.
findings.matters: A lender assessing Barnet's creditworthiness needs to know the council cannot fund day-to-day services from ordinary revenue. This signals structural financial distress and government dependence.
findings.figures: £79.6m capitalisation direction approved; £79.3m budget gap; £6.703m EFS financing costs in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: The council received confirmation on 22nd February 2026 that the Minister of State for Local Government and Homelessness is minded to approve a capitalisation direction of a total not exceeding £79.6 million for 2026/27.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: £400k permanent income loss from government-mandated Land Charges centralization, explicitly not replaced by alternative funding
findings.detail: The council is losing the ability to charge for LLC1 land searches as these are being centralized to the Land Registry. This is a government-mandated loss with no compensation: the document states the reduction is "not replaced by alternative funding." The pressure persists in 2027-28 (£50k).
findings.matters: This is structural income erosion imposed by government policy with no compensation. It signals similar pressures across all councils and indicates the local government funding system is shifting from councils generating their own income.
findings.figures: Land Charges income loss: £400,000 in 2026-27; £50,000 in 2027-28
findings.quote: As LLC1 searches are handed over to HMLR, local authorities lose the ability to charge for these searches, leading to a significant reduction in income that is not replaced by alternative funding. The £400K is the best estimate of our Local Land Charges subject matter expert

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Children and Family Services budget jumped 11% in one year (£88.2m to £97.8m) with continued pressures in looked-after children
findings.detail: The largest single service budget grew £9.5m. The council is explicitly 'rebasing' budgets for Independent Fostering Agencies (£375k), external residential placements (£475k), and Children with Disabilities respite (£500k), language that indicates prior budgets were set below actual demand and cost.
findings.matters: Double-digit annual growth in a major service budget with repeated 'rebasing' of demand-led services indicates structural cost pressures and prior underfunding that required correction.
findings.figures: 2025-26: £88,249,815; 2026-27: £97,794,523 (£9.5m growth, 10.8%). Pressures: IFA rebasing £375k, external residential rebasing £475k, CWD respite £500k, in-house foster carers £180k
findings.quote: To rebase the Independent Fostering Agencies budget in line with current demand pressure to provide robust starting point from which to take future savings from. These savings are expected to be delivered by reducing the proportion of looked after children in independent foster placements and increasing the use of more cost efficient in house fostering provision.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: A £250k savings proposal for Digital transformation is explicitly marked 'Undeliverable saving'
findings.detail: The Resources budget includes a line labelling a planned £250k saving from a digital Single Citizen View project as an undeliverable saving. This means a budgeted saving that the council now acknowledges cannot be delivered, creating a hidden gap that must be offset elsewhere.
findings.matters: Failed savings targets force councils to either overspend or find replacement cuts. An undeliverable saving signals either overoptimistic project forecasting or inability to complete planned digital investment.
findings.figures: Undeliverable saving: £250,000 in 2026-27
findings.quote: Undeliverable saving: Digital proposition relating to the development of a 'live' Single Citizen View, that can be used to check eligibility for Single Person Discount for Council Tax and detect potential fraud. 250,000 0 0 0 0

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy gap of £5.6m in 2026-27: council pays more than government permits it to claim subsidy for
findings.detail: A structural mismatch between HB costs and allowable subsidy creates a £5.627m pressure in 2026-27. The gap persists through 2029-30 (£1.484m), indicating this is not a temporary issue. The council identifies TA, supported accommodation, and overpayments as drivers, but these are largely outside its control.
findings.matters: This is a direct loss of expected government subsidy income outside council control. It represents funding erosion in a major benefit administration responsibility.
findings.quote: Budget was increased for 25/26 by £3m however forecasts at this point are suggesting an overspend of £3.2m. This pressure relates to the gap between HB paid out and subsidy we are permitted to claim. The largest gap relates to Temp Accommodation but supported accommodation and overpayments also result in gaps.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs have surged £5.7m in 2026-27, described as 'unprecedented increase over the last 2 years'
findings.detail: The budget shows a gross pressure of £5.677m for TA in 2026-27 alone, with forecasts declining only if multiple savings schemes (occupancy checks, move-ons to cheaper units, family mediation) all succeed. The council attributes this to higher nightly emergency accommodation rates and rising renewal prices. The persistence of £2.5m pressure even in 2029-30 suggests this remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled TA costs signal housing stress and homelessness the council cannot manage. Even with multiple simultaneous interventions, this remains the single largest pressure in the Growth directorate.
findings.figures: TA gross pressure 2026-27: £5,677,610; forecast to reduce to £4,358,000 (2027-28), £3,208,000 (2028-29), £2,470,000 (2029-30) if savings are delivered
findings.quote: Temporary Accomodation costs have seen an unprecedented increase over the last 2 years. The net cost of TA (TA costs less rental income) has increased due to demand and higher nightly paid emergency accommodation. Overall accommodation prices have increased so each renewal is at a higher rate.

findings.committee: Council
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Detailed Revenue Budgets, Savings and Income Generation, Pressures and Council Tax Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support rising from £55.727m to £79.298m in 2026/27; financing costs escalating to £22.611m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's 2026-27 budget depends on £79.3m of Exceptional Financial Support, up from £55.7m in 2025-26. More critically, the financing costs of this EFS grow dramatically each year: £6.7m in 2026-27, £9.6m in 2027-28, reaching £22.6m by 2030-31. This pattern of accumulating debt service costs suggests the council is taking on long-term borrowing to close annual deficits with no identified end point.
findings.matters: EFS financing costs show structural budget deficits. A council borrowing to balance each year and accruing £22.6m in annual debt service by year five is taking on commitments it must sustain indefinitely.

This meant full audit procedures could not be undertaken on the group financial statements for 2024/25, and the auditors were unable to complete work over group expenditure or conclude on fraud risks in group revenue.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee (GARMS)
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: Council failed to meet 30 June statutory deadline for accounts production, delivered 18 July, cascading audit delays to January 2026
findings.detail: The council did not meet the national deadline of 30 June for preparing financial statements. The final accounts were not received until 18 July, and supporting working papers were not produced on time, delaying the commencement and progression of audit work. Testing continued until January 2026 due to this delay, impacting the auditors' ability to complete planned procedures before the backstop date of 28 February 2026.
findings.matters: Late accounts production reduces time available for audit and creates artificial pressure on deadline compliance; cascading delays reduce audit quality and may force audit limitations.
findings.figures: 18-day delay on accounts production (30 June vs 18 July); audit testing extended to January 2026
findings.quote: The Council did not meet the national deadline of 30 June for preparing the financial statements. The final set of accounts was not received until 18 July

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee (GARMS)
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: Critical IT control deficiencies in Oracle system including inappropriate privileged access and GDPR non-compliance
findings.detail: Testing of Oracle system controls identified: 18 users with conflicting access across administrative, financial reporting, and payroll roles; 17 generic accounts with broad administrative privileges; 304 instances of self-assigned roles by 22 users with no retained approval evidence; no documented approvals for audit log changes; and no automated or documented data retention/deletion strategy creating GDPR non-compliance risks. Auditors conclude these "pose a risk of material misstatement, security incidents, and regulatory non-compliance."
findings.matters: IT control weaknesses create material risk of unauthorised changes to financial data; GDPR non-compliance creates regulatory penalty exposure; uncontrolled privileged access undermines the entire control environment.
findings.figures: 18 users with conflicting access; 17 generic accounts; 304 self-assigned role instances
findings.quote: 18 users had conflicting access across administrative, financial reporting, and payroll roles. This creates a material risk of unauthorised changes to financial data.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee (GARMS)
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: Approximately £7.9 million of unidentified cash receipts in debtor listings could not be tested
findings.detail: Within the debtor listing provided for audit, the auditors identified approximately £7.9 million of unidentified payments where cash had been receipted but not allocated to a customer or invoice. The listing contained transaction-level detail extending back more than one year with no allocation information available, preventing audit testing of these items.
findings.matters: Unidentified cash receipts indicate potential control weaknesses in income recording and reconciliation processes; they represent unresolved items that could mask revenue misstatements or collection issues.
findings.figures: £7.9 million unidentified payments
findings.quote: Unidentified cash receipts within debtor listings: Within the debtor listing, we identified approximately £7.9 million of unidentified payments, where cash had been receipted but not allocated.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee (GARMS)
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease implementation contains multiple material errors that auditors cannot conclude on
findings.detail: The council recognised £131.5m Right-of-Use assets and £135.12m lease liabilities in its first year of IFRS 16 implementation. Multiple categories of errors were identified: PFI scheme missing £6.214m transition adjustment; temporary accommodation leases incorrectly assessed as paid in advance when paid in arrears; peppercorn leases incorrectly recognised as liabilities instead of donated assets; and multiple leases incorrectly included as RoU assets. Adjustments made include £7.5m PFI opening balance adjustment, £6.37m RoU asset correction, and £2.956m long-term creditor restatement. Auditors conclude: "we are unable to conclude on the completeness and accuracy of the Authority's IFRS 16 accounting for 2024/25."
findings.matters: IFRS 16 leases represent a material balance sheet item; unresolved errors across multiple lease classifications indicate control weaknesses in accounting estimate processes and potential for further undetected misstatements.
findings.figures: £131.5m RoU assets; £135.12m lease liabilities; £7.5m PFI adjustment; £6.214m missing transition adjustment; £6.37m RoU asset restatement; £2.956m creditor restatement
findings.quote: Given the scale of the issues identified and the incomplete application of IFRS 16, we are unable to conclude on the completeness and accuracy of the Authority's IFRS 16 accounting for 2024/25.

findings.committee: Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee (GARMS)
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: £231m of external and agency pay costs could not be audited; transaction-level detail not provided in time
findings.detail: The council experienced difficulties extracting key payroll system reports from iTrent including gross-to-net reconciliation and starters/leavers reports. The required transaction-level detail was not provided in sufficient time to allow testing of external and agency pay costs before the backstop date. Related creditor balances for this expenditure were also not tested in full.
findings.matters: Payroll is one of the largest expenditure categories and a high-risk area for fraud and error; unaudited spend at this scale represents a major gap in financial assurance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Grant Thornton Audit Findings Report for the London Borough of Barnet 31 March 2025 (1)
findings.headline: Disclaimer of audit opinion will be issued for fourth consecutive year due to unaudited opening balances
findings.detail: The Authority has received disclaimed opinions since 2020/21. Opening balances for 2024/25 have not been audited, so auditors cannot conclude on overall financial position, reserves strategy, or reserve movements. The auditors state "the absence of assurance over opening balances fundamentally constrains the ability to issue an unqualified opinion for 2024/25."
findings.matters: No external validation of the council's financial position exists; lenders and the finance director cannot rely on audited financial statements to assess the council's financial health or borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Four years of disclaimers (2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2024/25)
findings.quote: The Authority has been subject to a disclaimer of audit opinion on its financial statements since 2020/21 under the Government's backstop arrangements.

findings.committee: Children and Education Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.paper_title: Children’s Services Quarterly Financial Update
findings.headline: Large aged debt from ICB of £4.673m over one year old, though agreement reached December 2025
findings.detail: Barnet is owed £8.150m by NHS bodies, of which £4.673m relates to ICB invoices from 2022/23 and 2023/24 for tripartite funding of external residential placements over £185k (33% of annual commitment to be funded by ICB). The council reached an agreement in December 2025 on both prior year and 2025/26 invoices, but the large aged balance indicates significant collection issues.
findings.matters: Large aged debts from health partners suggest disputes or payment difficulties in tripartite funding arrangements; though resolved now, it indicates cash-flow friction between partners.
findings.figures: £8.150m total, £4.673m aged over 1 year
findings.quote: Other Public Bodies balance outstanding of £8.150m includes £4.673m of aged debt greater than 1 year relating to ICB invoices raised in 2022/23 and 2023/24. These invoices are for tripartite funding for external residential placement packages over £185k

findings.committee: Children and Education Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.paper_title: Children’s Services Quarterly Financial Update
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block overspends by £5.928m, funded by drawing £5.668m from accumulated reserves
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £5.928m, with overspends in mainstream schools (£2.8m), independent sector (£2.0m), and Post 16 (£0.8m). This will be funded from DSG reserves brought forward of £8.305m. The paper identifies four persistent drivers: no maintained special school capacity, tribunal-directed placements, therapy capacity constraints, and rising complexity.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover recurring structural overspends signals the reserve is being used to fund ongoing costs, not one-off items, which is unsustainable without addressing the underlying causes.
findings.figures: £5.928m overspend, £5.668m funded from DSG reserves of £8.305m brought forward
findings.quote: The forecast overspend of £5.668m will be funded from DSG reserves brought forward of £8.305m

findings.committee: Children and Education Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.paper_title: Children’s Services Quarterly Financial Update
findings.headline: Average weekly placement fees have risen 37% in two years, now £7,780
findings.detail: The council is facing steep cost inflation in looked-after children placements, driven by increasing complexity of cases. The average weekly fee was £5,669 in 2023/24, rising to £7,322 in 2024/25 and now £7,780. The paper describes this as reflecting complex mental health and behavioural needs requiring solo provision and Deprivation of Liberty safeguards, and notes this is an ongoing nationwide cost pressure.
findings.matters: Placement costs are a major driver of council spending that reflect demand volatility outside the council's direct control; sustained inflation at this rate puts pressure on reserves and future budgets.
findings.quote: Average placement fees have increased dramatically: in 2023/24 the average weekly placement fee was £5,669 which rose to £7,322 in 2024/25 and is currently £7,780.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet used £45.9m of £55.7m government-approved support in 2025/26 and delivered 95.8% of savings
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council used £45.9m of the £55.7m in Exceptional Financial Support (government permission to borrow and sell assets to cover day-to-day spending) approved for 2025/26, about £10m less than allowed, according to papers for its Cabinet on 12 October. The council also delivered 95.8% of its planned savings and stayed within its agreed budget that year.

For 2026/27, the government has approved in principle up to £79.6m, of which £73.6m is expected to be needed. The council is seeking approval for 2027/28 and awaits clarification of the process from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Its Financial Sustainability Plan says support is likely to remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29. It sets a £200m target for financial benefits by 2029/30, against a forecast budget gap of £198m, with the aim of ending reliance on the support by March 2029. The papers say the plan's savings are not yet in the medium-term financial strategy (the council's five-year financial plan), and will be added once each has a business case, a named owner and delivery milestones.

The support must be repaid, and the borrowing carries yearly costs in interest and minimum revenue provision (the amount set aside each year to pay off past borrowing). These are put at £9.6m in 2027/28, rising to £13.2m, £17.4m and £22.6m in 2030/31, a total of £62.75m, before falling to zero in 2031/32. The council's papers also name social care demand, homelessness and housing benefit rates not updated since 2011 among the main pressures.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet delivered 95.8% of planned savings in 2025/26 and used £10m less government support than approved
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet delivered 95.8% of its planned savings in 2025/26, stayed within its agreed budget and used about £10m less exceptional financial support than government had approved. That support is permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The figures are in the council's financial sustainability plan, which goes to its Finance and Growth Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee. The same plan says the support "is likely to remain necessary in 2027/28 and potentially 2028/29".

The plan shows recurring savings and income building to £70m by 2027/28, £100m by 2028/29 and £200m by 2029/30. Residual support of £43m is forecast for 2027/28 and £49m for 2028/29, falling to nothing in 2029/30. The council's medium-term financial strategy, its financial plan for the next several years, forecasts a budget gap of £198m by 2029/30 because spending is expected to grow faster than income. The council aims to end its reliance on the support by March 2029. The strategy does not yet include any service savings from the plan. Proposals will be added once they have business cases, named owners and assessed delivery risks.

Borrowing carries a cost. Interest and minimum revenue provision, the amount set aside each year to pay off past borrowing, linked to the support rise from £9.552m in 2027/28 to £22.611m in 2030/31.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet forecasts needing £73.298m in exceptional government support for 2026-27, down £6m on plan
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council expects to need £73.298m of exceptional financial support (EFS) from government to balance its 2026-27 budget, £6m less than the £79.298m originally approved. EFS is permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort.

The figures are in a report on the financial outturn (the actual figures for the year just ended, compared with the budget) and 2026-27 budget management, prepared for the Children and Education Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee's meeting on 8 October 2026.

The report says the council "remains reliant" on EFS to balance this year's budget. The papers give the reduction in the forecast but, in the material reviewed, no breakdown of what produced it.
